description.sr_latin: Kako da se dogovoriš za izlazak, predložiš aktivnosti, i organizuješ bleju.
description.en: How to make plans, suggest activities, and organize hangouts.

phrases.context: Suggesting a night out. 'Hajde da' + verb is the standard way to say 'let's'.
phrases.notes: 'Izađemo' comes from 'izaći' (to go out). Very common for suggesting plans.

phrases.context: Suggesting a casual walk. Šetnja (a walk) is a big part of Serbian social life.
phrases.notes: 'Prošetamo' = 'take a stroll'. Serbians love evening walks, especially along the river or through town.

phrases.context: Suggesting drinks. Deliberately vague about whether it's coffee, beer, or rakija.
Suggesting a movie or show at home.

phrases.en: Do you want to go out?
phrases.context: Asking someone if they want to go out — works for both a date and hanging with friends.

phrases.en: Can we go to the cinema?
phrases.context: Suggesting a movie. 'Bioskop' = cinema/movie theater.

phrases.sr_latin: Ima jedan dobar restoran blizu, hoćeš da probamo?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Има један добар ресторан близу, хоћеш да пробамо?
phrases.en: There's a good restaurant nearby, want to try it?
phrases.context: Suggesting a new place to eat.
Quick, casual invite for after-work drinks. 'Aj' is the ultra-casual form of 'hajde'.
phrases.notes: 'Aj' is even shorter than 'ajde'. Peak casual Serbian.

phrases.en: What are you doing this weekend?
phrases.context: The classic Friday question to friends or your partner.

phrases.sr_latin: Imaš li neke planove za vikend?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Имаш ли неке планове за викенд?
phrases.en: Do you have any plans for the weekend?
phrases.context: A slightly more formal way to ask about weekend plans.
The standard non-answer to weekend plan questions.

phrases.en: Shall we go somewhere this weekend?
phrases.context: Open-ended suggestion for a weekend trip or outing.
Inviting friends over to chill. 'Bleja' is slang for hanging out/chilling.
phrases.notes: 'Bleja' comes from 'blejati' which literally means 'to bleat' (like a sheep). It's evolved into the most common word for just hanging out and doing nothing.

phrases.context: Inviting a group of friends over. 'Dođite' is plural/polite 'come'.
When you don't need a plan — just hanging out is the plan.
The most common way to accept any plan or invitation. Short and enthusiastic.
phrases.notes: 'Može' is probably the most useful single word in Serbian. It means 'okay', 'sure', 'can do', 'deal'.

phrases.context: Confirming plans. 'Važi' = 'it's valid/agreed' but used casually like 'cool/alright'.
phrases.notes: 'Važi' is another essential word. You'll hear it constantly.

phrases.context: Expressing excitement about upcoming plans.
Confirming you'll meet at the agreed location.

phrases.sr_latin: Ne mogu danas, jel' može sutra?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Не могу данас, јел' може сутра?
phrases.en: I can't today, how about tomorrow?
phrases.context: Declining but offering an alternative. Keeps the door open.

phrases.en: It'll have to be another time.
phrases.context: Politely declining when you're not available.
The honest excuse. Use 'Umorna sam' if female.

variations.en: I can't be bothered to go out.

phrases.en: What are you doing? / What's up?
phrases.context: The most common conversation opener in Serbian. Can mean 'what are you doing right now' or just 'hey, what's up'.
phrases.notes: This is often used as a greeting, not just a literal question.

phrases.en: Where are you? / Hey, what's up?
phrases.context: Can be literal ('where are you?') or a casual greeting meaning 'hey!'.
phrases.notes: When used as a greeting, it doesn't actually require you to state your location.

phrases.context: Checking availability before suggesting plans. Use 'slobodna' for female.
Asking when to meet.
Suggesting a time. 'Recimo' = 'let's say'.
phrases.notes: Serbians tend to run late, so 'u osam' might mean 8:15-8:30.

phrases.en: I'm running a bit late, wait for me.
phrases.context: The text you'll send when you're already supposed to be there.
phrases.notes: 'Malo' = 'a little'. Could mean 5 minutes, could mean 30.

phrases.context: Deciding on a meeting point.
Convincing someone to come along. 'Bre' is a uniquely Serbian exclamation — an all-purpose interjection.
phrases.notes: 'Bre' has no direct translation. It adds emphasis, like 'man', 'dude', or just raw energy. Quintessentially Serbian.

phrases.en: What are you waiting for? Let's go!
phrases.context: Pushing someone to stop thinking and just go.

phrases.en: Oh come on, what's stopping you.
phrases.context: Persuading someone who's on the fence. 'Šta ti fali' = 'what are you missing/lacking'.
phrases.notes: 'Ma' before 'hajde' adds an insistent, almost exasperated tone.

phrases.context: Finalizing plans. Clean, definitive.

phrases.en: I'll text you when I leave.
phrases.context: Letting someone know you'll update them when you're on your way.
phrases.notes: 'Javim' = 'I'll let you know/inform'. Very commonly used for coordination.

phrases.context: Asking someone to let you know when they get there.
The standard casual goodbye when you have plans to meet.

variations.en: Talk later! / We'll be in touch!
